output.solution_body: Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that $S$ contains no increasing subsequence of length $n+1$ and no decreasing subsequence of length $n+1$. Then for every $i \in \{1, 2, \dots, n^2+1\}$, we must have $1 \le a_i \le n$ and $1 \le b_i \le n$. The set of all possible coordinate pairs is therefore a subset of the Cartesian product $\{1, 2, \dots, n\} \times \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$, which contains exactly $n \cdot n = n^2$ distinct elements.\n\nHowever, by Lemma 2, the mapping $i \mapsto (a_i, b_i)$ is strictly injective, meaning each of the $n^2+1$ elements of $S$ is mapped to a unique pair. By the Pigeonhole Principle, $n^2+1$ distinct elements cannot be injectively mapped into a set of size $n^2$. This contradiction completes the proof: $S$ must contain at least one monotonic subsequence of length $n+1$.
